title: Context may be the new material of product design
description: With AI and agents, the system needs to understand context. How designers start designing relationships, rules and supervision, not just screens.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: AI agents that act inside the CRM and keep the person in control.

blocks.text: For a long time, we thought of UX work as creating screens, flows, journeys and components.
But products are changing.
With generative AI and agents, the system also needs to understand context.

items: It needs to know what is happening
What that person is trying to do
And which decisions can or cannot be made

blocks.text: This creates a new opportunity for design:
designing not just interfaces, but also the context that guides intelligent systems.
What happens when the interface stops being the center?
Imagine you want to reschedule a trip.

blocks.caption: The unit of design kept growing, from the screen to the agent.

blocks.text: In a traditional product, you would probably go through several screens:
Trip → Booking → Change date → Choose flight → Confirm.
Now imagine you simply say:
“I need to move my flight to Friday night.”
An agent can interpret the intent and handle part of the process.
The interface still exists.
But it is no longer the only place where the interaction happens.
The system needs to understand the intent.
And that changes the design problem.
Information is not enough. The system needs context.

data.lead: Imagine an agent that receives the message:
data.a: Cancel what? The sentence alone is not enough.

blocks.text: This is where it gets interesting to think about something close to a context architecture.
If information architecture organizes content so people can find what they need, context architecture helps intelligent systems understand which information to consider before acting.
Designers start designing relationships

data.chainA: Screen A → Screen B → Screen C
data.b: Now we may need to think:
data.chainB: Intent → context → rules → data → action → confirmation

blocks.text: That is different.
The designer needs to consider what information the system needs to make a decision.
For example, a user asks to cancel a subscription.
The system may need to know:

items: whether there is a minimum term;
whether there is a pending charge;

blocks.text: All of this is part of the experience.
Even if the user never sees all of this information on a screen.
Context can also be wrong
If the system understands the wrong context, it can make the wrong decision.
That is why agent experiences need to show more than just the result.

data.lead: They need to help the user understand:
questions: Why did it make that decision?
data.after: This transparency starts to become part of UX.

blocks.text: Control becomes even more important
In a traditional interface, the user usually performs the actions.
In a more autonomous system, the system can take actions on its own.
That changes the relationship.
If an agent can send a message, make a booking or change a setting, we need to think about levels of autonomy.
Maybe some actions can be automatic.
Others need confirmation.
And some should require explicit approval.
Design needs to define these limits.
Not every automation needs to be automatic
When we can automate something, there is a tendency to automate it.
But the question should be:
Should this action be automatic?
Imagine a finance app.
Running an automatic analysis can be great.
Transferring a large amount without confirmation is another story.
An agent can find a travel option.
Buying that ticket automatically is a different decision.
The bigger the impact of the action, the greater the need for control and confirmation may be.
The new flow may be intent → action → supervision
In traditional products, we think a lot about:

blocks.caption: Why agent UX is different from putting a chatbot in the interface.

blocks.text: input → interface → action
In agent experiences, we can start thinking about:
intent → interpretation → action → feedback → supervision
This flow changes the role of the interface quite a bit.
The interface may stop being the place where every action happens.
It can become the place where the user follows, corrects, approves or understands what the system is doing.
This also changes information architecture
If an agent needs to access different information to answer or perform a task, that information needs to be organized in a way that makes sense.
Having content is not enough.
We need to think about:
This brings UX closer to areas that used to seem far away.
Designers start taking part in these conversations because they directly affect the experience.
Context may be a new kind of Design System
This is a provocation.

blocks.caption: Just like tokens, context can also be organized in layers.

blocks.text: A traditional Design System defines components, patterns and visual rules.
But imagine a system where we also have context rules:
When should this information be used?
Who can access it?
Which information takes priority?
When should we ask for confirmation?
What to do when there is ambiguity?
How to handle an exception?
This does not replace a Design System.
But it widens the conversation.
We are starting to design not only how the product looks, but how it should behave in different situations.
Designers need to understand the whole system
This shift reinforces something that was already happening in Product Design.
Designers can't look only at the screen.
They need to understand:
What happens before?
What happens after?
What data is involved?
What are the rules?
Who makes the decision?
What happens when something goes wrong?
Who can fix it?
What is the impact of that action?
This systemic view becomes even more important when the product starts acting on its own.
And where does research come in?
We need to understand:
How do people describe their intentions?
When do they want autonomy?
When do they prefer control?
What kinds of errors are acceptable?
What makes a person trust a recommendation?
When do they want to review an action?
These answers shouldn't be decided by technology alone.
We need to study how people behave.
We are designing experiences, not just interfaces
Maybe this is the main change.
For a long time, the designer's unit of work was the screen.
Then we started thinking about flows and journeys.
Now we also need to think about systems that interpret, recommend and act.
This increases the responsibility of design.
But it also opens a huge space for Product Designers.
Because someone needs to organize this experience.
Someone needs to decide where autonomy exists.

items: Someone needs to think about feedback
Someone needs to understand the user

blocks.text: And someone needs to make sure technology keeps making sense for people.
